lines.text: Capstone time! Today you turn everything from Level 2 into your own AI work playbook, and you prove what it saves.
For one normal week, list every task that takes more than fifteen minutes, with how often you do it and how long it takes.
Group the tasks into messages, reports, data, documents and meetings.
This is your time map.
Score each task on minutes per week, how repetitive it is, and how risky a mistake would be.
Choose three tasks that are frequent, repetitive and low to medium risk.
Leave high-risk decisions about people, money, health and the law with people.
Match each task to a tool from this course: a template, a mail merge, a dashboard, a form with a summary, a script, or a role prompt kit.
Add a human checkpoint to each one.
Test with practice or anonymised data first.
Log before and after times for each task, including checks and setup.
Then write five to eight responsible-use rules for your own work, covering privacy, checking, honesty, labelling and who approves.
Your playbook is the tasks, the tools, the numbers and the rules together.
Show your time map, your three automations, one mistake a checkpoint caught, and the hours saved per month.
Finish with your rules, what you will automate next, and what you will never hand to AI.
Start with a simple sheet of every task that takes more than fifteen minutes in a normal week.
Give each task a score for how repetitive it is and how risky a mistake would be.
A simple formula ranks the tasks, and high-risk work stays with people.
Your top three tasks become the heart of your playbook.
Claude matches each of the three tasks to a tool from the course, with a checkpoint.
The table is sensible, and every task keeps a person in the loop.
But the tip at the end says to message every customer every morning, with no review.
That removes the checkpoint and could spam people, so we keep the preview step.
Now we ask ChatGPT to help draft six rules for our own job.
Most of the rules are strong: privacy, checking, labelling, approvals and people decisions.
But rule four says template messages need no checking, and that is exactly how broken merges get sent.
We rewrite it, because these are our rules, and we stand behind every line.
Six slides are enough: the map, three automations, the numbers, and your rules.
Every automation slide shows before, after, the checkpoint, and one real catch.
Rehearse with a timer, and only show practice or anonymised data.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now plan it, build it, test it, and share it!
